steps.title: Close the cold inlet valve
steps.text: Turn the shutoff valve on top of the cold water line clockwise to stop fresh water from feeding the leak.

steps.text: Switch off the water heater breaker at the panel or turn the gas control knob to off.

symptoms.title: Water pooling beneath the tank
symptoms.text: Rusty water seeping from the bottom jacket seam usually indicates internal tank corrosion that cannot be patched.

symptoms.title: Frequent repeat breakdowns
symptoms.text: Replacing multiple elements, thermostats, or valves on an aging unit often signals the tank is nearing the end of its life.

symptoms.title: Visible rust on fittings or tank
symptoms.text: Heavy exterior corrosion around top nipples, the drain valve, or the flue collar suggests advanced internal wear.

symptoms.title: Lukewarm water despite repairs
symptoms.text: Severe mineral buildup can choke tank volume and recovery so badly that replacement becomes more practical than flushing.

symptoms.title: Household outgrew tank size
symptoms.text: Adding family members or bathrooms often makes a 40-gallon tank feel undersized during back-to-back morning showers.

symptoms.title: Rusty hot water from multiple taps
symptoms.text: Discolored water only on the hot side points to a failing tank lining rather than your home's cold supply pipes.

phoenixAngle.heading: Sizing & Permit Considerations in Phoenix
paragraphs: Phoenix's hard water wears down tank linings and anode rods faster than soft-water regions, making timely replacement important before a basement or garage pan overflows. Garage temperatures in summer also mean cold-water inlet temperatures vary seasonally, affecting how quickly a tank recovers after back-to-back morning showers.

Homeowners often ask about local permits when swapping a water heater. Rules differ by city and by the specific work being done. Your plumber will tell you whether a permit applies, and City of Phoenix residential guidelines distinguish contractor replacements from DIY electric swaps.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to replace a water heater in Phoenix?
faqs.a: Rules differ by city and by the work being done. Your plumber will tell you whether a permit applies. According to the City of Phoenix residential permits page, water heater replacements completed by a licensed contractor are listed differently from DIY electric replacements or fixture relocations.

faqs.q: What size water heater does a typical Phoenix home need?
faqs.a: Most two-to-three bathroom homes use a 40-gallon or 50-gallon tank, while larger households with soaking tubs or simultaneous showers may prefer a 50-gallon high-recovery or 75-gallon model. We review your bathroom count and peak hot water habits on the phone.

faqs.q: Should I switch to tankless during my replacement?
faqs.a: A tankless unit saves space and delivers continuous hot water, but it often requires larger gas piping, updated stainless venting, and dedicated hard-water descaling. If you want a simple swap with lower upfront complexity, a standard tank is usually more straightforward.

faqs.q: Do you haul away the old leaking water heater?
faqs.a: Yes. Once we drain and disconnect your failed water heater, we remove the old tank from your property as part of the replacement service so you are not left dealing with a heavy, rusted appliance sitting in your garage or side yard.

faqs.q: Can my old water heater just be repaired instead?
faqs.a: If the tank body itself is dry and the problem is a thermostat, heating element, or valve, repair is often practical. Once the inner steel tank corrodes and leaks through the bottom or side seam, replacement is the only safe option.

faqs.q: How can I make my new water heater last longer in Phoenix?
faqs.a: Periodic tank flushing to clear mineral sediment, checking the sacrificial anode rod, and installing a whole-home water softener can reduce hard-water wear. Ask our plumber about practical maintenance options suited to your home's water quality, tank size, and daily usage.
